title: Working backwards through operations
transcript: Work backwards when you know where an operation ended but need to find where it began. Each step has an inverse that restores its input. For a chain of changes, undo the last change first. Then test the whole forward chain.

An AMC Upper Primary problem may tell you what happened to a mystery number, a balance or a pile and ask for the starting amount. A Rossmoyne style question can also constrain the final range or require whole numbers along the way. Reverse only the legal states.
A machine adds three to a number, then multiplies by three. The final output is twenty-seven. What went in? Trace from the right of the diagram to the left.

Undo the multiplication by dividing twenty-seven by three. The result is nine, just after the original addition. Now subtract three to find the input six. As a check, forward addition and multiplication return twenty-seven.

Remove one of four equal parts of a pile. Then add five counters. There are twenty-six counters afterwards. How many were in the pile at the start? Write the intermediate state before restoring the whole.

Subtract the addition of five. That leaves twenty-one, which is three of the original four equal parts. Divide those twenty-one counters by three. One original part has seven counters. Rebuild the original four parts. There were twenty-eight counters before either operation.

Start with a positive whole number. Add two, multiply by three, divide by two, and subtract four. The final reading is a whole number from twenty-three to thirty-two inclusive. Find all possible whole-number inputs.

Take each possible reading, add four, then multiply by two. We are undoing the final two operations. An input can be whole only if that intermediate result is divisible by three. Check the readings against this condition before going further. The allowed readings are twenty-three, twenty-six, twenty-nine and thirty-two. Undo the first two operations for those readings only.

Divide each allowed intermediate value by three, then subtract two. This gives sixteen, eighteen, twenty and twenty-two. For example, starting at sixteen and running all four steps forward gives twenty-three. Every reading in the requested interval was tested.

Undo multiplication with division, and undo addition with subtraction. Reversing just the signs without reversing the order changes the input. A fraction refers to the whole at the time it was used. Check how many equal parts the intermediate value represents.

Write a short arrow for every step. Work from the known output, writing the inverse of the last arrow first. Check required whole numbers and allowed ranges as you reverse. Confirm your answer by running each claimed input forward.
